Introduction

blocks.text: Sports video understanding has received significant attention due to its wide applications in analytics [28], coaching [12], officiating support [15, 16], content retrieval [44], and audience engagement [29]. Recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) [1, 2, 5, 21, 36] demonstrate strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, †Corresponding author. ∗This work was done when K. Chen was an intern at Microsoft Research Asia. making them promising for sports video analysis. However, sports videos pose unique challenges for MLLMs, such as rapid movements, dense player interactions, domainspecific rules, and the need for fine-grained subtle visual cues. Several benchmarks have been developed to study sports video understanding, such as SoccerNet [11], Sports- QA [22], and multi-sport datasets [41, 42]. While these benchmarks advance holistic understanding of broadcast videos, they typically assume that a single camera view provides sufficient evidence for question answering (QA). In real-world, sports events are captured from multiple viewpoints to provide a complete perspective for referees and audiences. Occlusion is common in sports: players often cluster around decisive moments, making critical actions hard to observe from a single view. Moreover, athletes may intentionally obscure events through exaggerated contact or simulated falls, making single-view evidence not only incomplete but sometimes misleading. blocks.text: Sports understanding benchmarks.Early sports understanding datasets primarily focused on action classification or action quality assessment in specific sports like soccer [11], basketball [43], diving [23], gymnastics [34] and figure skating [25]. Later datasets expanded the task from simple action classification to temporal action parsing [26, 33] and spatio-temporal localization [43], and also introduced a wider variety of sports categories [24]. With the advent of MLLMs [7–9, 27, 45], questionanswering (QA) benchmarks emerged as the standard paradigm for evaluating multimodal understanding in sports scenarios. blocks.text: In this section, we presentSportMV-Bench, a benchmark for multi-view sports video understanding designed to evaluate the capabilities of MLLMs in multi-view scenarios. We detail its problem formulation, data construction pipeline and resulting data statistics. Problem formulation.We consider the task of multi-view sports video understanding. Let V={V 1, V2, . . . , VN }denoteNvideos capturing the same sports event from different camera viewpoints, which may not be temporally synchronized. Given a naturallanguage questionq, the goal is to infer the correct answer aby aggregating evidence across the multi-view videos. Each question is formulated as a multiple-choice problem with candidate setA={a 1, a2, . . . , aK}, where a single ground-truth answera ∗ is annotated and verified by human experts.

Stage 2: LLM-Based QA proposal.Each referee report collected in Stage 1 can serve as the factual answer source. We feed it to an LLM and instruct it to simulate a referee certification exam setter. For each report, the model needs to propose multiple-choice questions strictly grounded in the report and produce one gold answer copied from the report. Distractors are required to be of the same semantic type as the gold answer and to be minimally contrasting variants drawn from non-deciding details in the same report, so that guessing by type mismatch is avoided. The prompt enforces no external knowledge, no hallucinated entities, and a fixed JSON-formatted output containing the question, options, and gold answer, denoted as the tuple(q,A, a ∗). Each synthesized item is linked to the corresponding multiview clips for later multimodal verification. In fact, we also attempted to condition the MLLM on both the referee report and the associated video clip for QA synthesis, but the results were suboptimal. Please see the supplementary material for more details. Stage 3: Multimodal verification.Despite the instruction constraints in Stage 2, a subset of synthesized QA items still deviate from the referee report, are inferable by commonsense alone, are unrelated to the video, or lack sufficient visual evidence to be inferable. For each candidate tuple (q,A, a∗)with the referee reportRand multi-view clipsV, the auditor is prompted to 1) verify whether the predicted answer is consistent with theR; 2) determine whether the item is commonsense-inferable, 3) check whether the QA pair is semantically aligned with the video content, and 4) assess whether the answer can be inferred from the video. We define a visual-inferable confidence score∈[0,10]to quantify this verification process. Instances that fail either the consistency and commonsense check, or fall below the confidence threshold, are filtered out. To reduce artifacts, the audit is repeated three times with the view order shuffled, and an item must pass all audits to be accepted. Stage 4: Authoritative manual filtering.Finally, expert annotators review the remaining items to remove ambiguous, non-visual, weakly grounded, or ill-posed questions, and to refine the wording and options so that the gold answer is clear and unique. The resulting corpus attains high precision in linguistic form and multimodal alignment, providing a robust basis for evaluating multi-view, fine-grained visual–textual understanding in sports officiating contexts.

Producing the correct answer requires aggregating complementary evidence across views, thereby evaluating an MLLM’s capability to understand and reason over multi-camera sports footage. blocks.text: which account for34.61%,38.23%, and27.16%of the corpus, respectively. These categories reflect increasing levels of reasoning and dependence on multi-view evidence. We detail each category as follows: •Perception-Aware Recognition (PAR).Evaluates lowlevel perceptual grounding ofwhat happenedacross views (e.g., tackle, block, push). The focus is on robust action identification under occlusion, motion blur, or adverse framing, benefiting from cross-view corroboration. •Rule Event Aware Interpretation (REI).Probes midlevel, event/rule-sensitive reasoning: REI consists of questions whose interpretation depends on rule or eventbased anchors specified in the query itself. Models are required to localize these anchors in space and time from different view clips and then obtain rule or event-related answers about what happens before or after these anchors. •Adjudicative Decision Reasoning (ADR).Assesses high-level normative inference by synthesizing multicamera views to concludewhat should be called. This involves localizing the foul context (e.g., inside vs. outside the box), estimating severity and intent, and mapping the situation to the appropriate sanction (yellow/red card, free kick, penalty, flagrant) without any explicit hints, thereby rigorously testing cross-view spatiotemporal integration and rule-grounded decision making. In summary, SportMV-Bench is the first benchmark that requires MLLMs to jointly reason across multiple asynchronous camera views of the same sports event. Its three-

blocks.text: As analyzed in Sec. 4, existing MLLMs struggle with multiview sports understanding. A single forward pass forces the model to passively process all perspectives at once, including occlusion and misleading evidence. We instead adopt an agentic approach:SportMV-Agentactively decides which view to examine, invokes specialized perception tools to extract concrete evidence, and iteratively accumulates findings until sufficient confidence is reached. Overview.As illustrated in Fig. 6, SportMV-Agent takes as input a questionq, multi-view videosV, and a set of perception toolsT, and outputs the predicted answerˆa. The framework consists of an orchestrator that coordinates an iterative loop ofevidence collectionandevidence-grounded reasoning, continuing until sufficient evidence is gathered for a confident prediction.

Active tool selection and execution.Fine-grained perception is demonstrated to be critical for multi-view sports understanding. We equip the framework with a Perception ToolboxTthat delivers sports-specific expertise asperceptionrather than text. The orchestrator invokes these tools through the operationo t =TOOLEXEC, which selects the appropriate tool and target view based on the current state. The toolbox are extendable and currently includes three fundamental tools designed for sports analysis: •Action Recognition(T act): outputs a ranked list of action names with confidence scores. •Contact Detection(T con): outputs a binary judgment of whether physical contact occurs between two players. •Contact Part Detection(T par): triggered when contact is detected, outputs the body region involved. For example, given a football play question, the orchestrator may start from a global view to identify the foul area. Realizing that the specific action type and physical contact is obscured, it triggers a view switch to a close-up sideline angle, invokesT act to categorize the type of action, and then invokesT con to determine the situation of contact before emitting a final decision.

blocks.text: We report the main quantitative results in Tab. 1. Among all the baseline MLLMs, GPT-4.1 achieves the best performance at 59.68%. For the open-source models, GLM-4.5V leads with 49.79%, but still lags substantially behind proprietary models. Notably, models with strong general video understanding capabilities, such as Qwen3-VL-30B, show a performance drop on our multi-view benchmark, highlighting the unique challenges of multi-perspective sports reasoning. A category-wise results reveal that most models excel in REI but struggle with PAR and ADR, with average performance gaps of about 9.2% and 21.1%, respectively. As identified in Sec. 4, REI often depends on a single decisive cue, while PAR suffers from occlusion and ADR requires cross-view evidence integration with rule-based reasoning. heading_path: Beyond the Single Camera: Agentic Multi-View Reasoning

Conclusion

blocks.text: In this paper, we introduce SportMV-Bench, the first multiview benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs on multiview sports video understanding. SportMV-Bench is built from real-world sports match videos, covers three primary question types, and contains 2,592 QA pairs that have been dual filtered by an MLLM and human annotators. Experiments reveal that current models often fail to select decisive viewpoints, perform precise perception, and aggregate complementary evidence, leading to large gaps in multiview sports understanding. To address these challenges, we present SportMV-Agent, an agentic framework equipped with an active view selection mechanism and the ability to invoke various perception tools. We hope this challenge benchmark will foreground the importance of multi-view evidence in sports video understanding and promote methods that advance robust multi-view reasoning in MLLMs for real-world applications. 9

blocks.text: As mentioned in the main paper, using MLLMs as a QA generator can yield undesirable items once visual input is introduced. As illustrated in Fig. 13, CoT fails to provide a correct ruling for this complex ADR case. blocks.text: D. More Implementation Details
heading_path: Beyond the Single Camera: Agentic Multi-View Reasoning
D. More Implementation Details

blocks.text: As mentioned in the main paper, we leverage Qwen2.5-VL- 72B [2] as the action recognition tool, contact detection tool and contact part detection tool in our proposed agentic framework. The output of the action recognition and contact part detection tool comprises the Top-3 retrieval results and their corresponding confidence scores. In this section, we will provide more details. For action recognition, we restrict the model’s output space to the predefined action taxonomies of the respective datasets. Specifically, for soccer tasks, the model is constrained to the action classes defined in SoccerNet[11]; for basketball tasks, it is limited to the categories within FineSports[43]. This definition of action sets is comprehensive enough for the relevant sports categories, effectively preventing ’open-set’ hallucinations and facilitating a more objective evaluation of the reasoning pipeline. For the contact part detection tool, we employ a hierarchical classification strategy. E. Future Outlook

blocks.text: In main paper, we demonstrate that the precise visual perception is essential to multi-view sports understanding. However, during our experiments, we observed that the model exhibits notable deficiencies in basic perceptual understanding of sports, even when we only provide a single favorable camera viewpoint. As illustrated in Fig. 12, MLLM often fails to distinguish between standing tackles and sliding tackles. This suggests that there remains substantial room to improve the foundational training of MLLMs on perceptual skills, calling for more systematic and fine-grained research in this domain. Moreover, the multi-view setting explored in this work can naturally be extended to a broader range of sports, such as American football and volleyball, which feature complex tactical structures and rich multi-agent interactions. However, constructing and releasing such datasets at scale poses significant challenges, including copyright, privacy, and collection cost. We therefore envision future collaborations with official sports organizations and broadcasters to build highquality, standardized multi-view sports video benchmarks, and to jointly advance research on multi-view sports video understanding. 14
